title: Existence of a Simple Graph of Order 20 with a Non-Unimodal Zero Forcing Polynomial
abstract: The zero forcing polynomial $\mathcal{Z}(G; x) = \sum_{i=1}^n z(G, i) x^i$ of a graph $G$ of order $n$ counts its zero forcing sets by size. Whether it is always unimodal was asked in earlier work; arXiv:2611.11352 answered no with an infinite family, its smallest member having order 81, and asked for the smallest graph with a non-unimodal zero forcing polynomial. We give an explicit graph of order 20 whose zero forcing polynomial is not unimodal: Lean proves $z(G,15) \ge 932$, $z(G,16) \le 909$ and $z(G,17) \ge 939$, so the coefficients dip at 16. Exhaustive enumeration gives the whole polynomial, $420x^{14}+932x^{15}+909x^{16}+939x^{17}+180x^{18}+20x^{19}+x^{20}$. This brings the known upper bound on the smallest order from 81 down to 20.
introduction:
Zero forcing is a dynamic process on a graph that models the spread of information or color across vertices. Starting with an initial subset of vertices that are colored, the color change rule dictates that a colored vertex with exactly one uncolored neighbor forces that neighbor to become colored. A subset of vertices whose iterative closure under this rule colors all vertices in the graph is called a zero forcing set. The zero forcing number of a graph is the minimum cardinality of a zero forcing set, and it provides bounds on the maximum nullity of symmetric matrices associated with the graph.

Beyond the minimum cardinality, the distribution of all zero forcing sets by size provides a detailed combinatorial profile of the graph. For a finite simple graph $G = (V, E)$ of order $n = |V|$, this distribution is encoded in the zero forcing polynomial:
$$\mathcal{Z}(G; x) = \sum_{i=1}^n z(G, i) x^i,$$
where $z(G, i)$ denotes the number of zero forcing sets of $G$ having cardinality $i$. The polynomial $\mathcal{Z}(G; x)$ is a generating function of zero forcing sets, with $z(G, i) = 0$ for all $i$ strictly less than the zero forcing number of $G$, and $z(G, n) = 1$ since the full vertex set $V$ always forms a zero forcing set.

A central question in the study of combinatorial polynomials is unimodality. A polynomial with non-negative real coefficients is called unimodal if its sequence of coefficients non-decreases up to a maximum index (a mode) and non-increases thereafter. Many classical graph polynomials, such as matching polynomials, independence polynomials for certain graph classes, and chromatic polynomials under suitable transformations, exhibit unimodality or log-concavity. Whether the zero forcing polynomial $\mathcal{Z}(G; x)$ is unimodal for every finite simple graph $G$ was asked in earlier work, which also showed that the first half of the coefficient sequence is always non-decreasing.

In arXiv:2611.11352, it was shown that zero forcing polynomials are not unimodal in general. The paper introduced an explicit family of constructions and showed that a specific graph denoted $G_{24,24,23}$ has order 81 and possesses a non-unimodal zero forcing polynomial. The family itself is non-unimodal from order 82 on; the order-81 graph is a smaller variant of it.

Section 3 of arXiv:2611.11352 then poses Question 2: "What is the smallest graph with a non-unimodal zero forcing polynomial?" The order-81 graph was the smallest example known, so a first step is whether a counterexample of order at most 80 exists at all.

This post presents a formal verification settling the order-at-most-80 question. We describe the theorem `op_1400_counterexample_order_le_eighty`, verified in the Lean 4 proof assistant, which proves that there exists a simple graph $G$ on Fin $n$ with $n \le 80$ whose zero forcing polynomial is not unimodal. In fact, the witness graph has order $n = 20$, which is substantially smaller than the threshold of 80 and the original counterexample of order 81. The polynomial of this 20-vertex graph is:
$$\mathcal{Z}(G; x) = 420 x^{14} + 932 x^{15} + 909 x^{16} + 939 x^{17} + 180 x^{18} + 20 x^{19} + x^{20}.$$
The coefficient sequence exhibits a drop from $z(G, 15) \ge 932$ to $z(G, 16) \le 909$, followed by an increase to $z(G, 17) \ge 939$. This interior dip mathematically precludes unimodality.
result:
The main theorem resolves the order-at-most-80 question by exhibiting an explicit counterexample of order 20.

Theorem (`op_1400_counterexample_order_le_eighty`):
There exists a natural number $n \le 80$ and a simple graph $G$ on the vertex set Fin $n$ with decidable adjacency relation whose zero forcing polynomial is not unimodal:
$$\exists (n : \mathbb{N})\; (\_ : n \le 80)\; (G : \text{SimpleGraph } (\text{Fin } n))\; (\_ : \text{DecidableRel } G.\text{Adj}),\; \neg\, \text{polynomial_is_unimodal } (\text{zero_forcing_poly } G).$$

The Lean statement `op_1400_counterexample_order_le_eighty` reads the English theorem by existentially quantifying over a natural number $n$, an inequality constraint $n \le 80$, a simple graph $G$ on the type Fin $n$, and an instance of decidable adjacency DecidableRel $G\text{.Adj}$, asserting that the zero forcing polynomial `zero_forcing_poly` $G$ is not unimodal according to `polynomial_is_unimodal`.

The witness graph $G$ has vertex set $\{0, \dots, 19\}$ and 135 edges: two distinct vertices are adjacent unless they form one of the following 55 pairs,
$${0,1}, {0,4}, {0,5}, {0,6}, {0,8}, {0,9}, {1,8}, {1,9}, {2,3}, {2,7}, {2,8}, {2,9}, {3,7}, {3,8}, {3,9}, {4,5}, {4,6}, {4,7}, {5,6}, {5,7}, {6,7}, {10,11}, {10,12}, {10,13}, {10,14}, {10,15}, {10,16}, {10,17}, {11,12}, {11,13}, {11,14}, {11,15}, {11,16}, {11,17}, {12,13}, {12,14}, {12,15}, {12,16}, {12,17}, {13,15}, {13,16}, {13,17}, {13,19}, {14,15}, {14,16}, {14,17}, {14,19}, {15,16}, {15,17}, {15,18}, {15,19}, {16,17}, {16,18}, {16,19}, {17,18}.$$
Its twin classes (vertices with the same neighbours outside the pair) are $\{2,3\}$, $\{4,5,6\}$, $\{8,9\}$, $\{10,11,12\}$, $\{13,14\}$, $\{15,16\}$ and six singletons, so $G$ is a blow-up of a 12-vertex graph. By exhaustive enumeration (a computation outside Lean), its zero forcing polynomial is:
$$\mathcal{Z}(G; X) = 420 X^{14} + 932 X^{15} + 909 X^{16} + 939 X^{17} + 180 X^{18} + 20 X^{19} + X^{20}.$$
So its zero forcing number is 14. Lean does not prove these exact values; it proves the three bounds below, which are all that non-unimodality needs.

The non-unimodality of $G$ is witnessed by the three coefficients at degrees 15, 16, and 17, which satisfy:
$$z(G, 15) \ge 932,\quad z(G, 16) \le 909,\quad z(G, 17) \ge 939.$$
Because $z(G, 15) > z(G, 16)$ and $z(G, 16) < z(G, 17)$, the coefficient sequence dips strictly at index 16. If the polynomial were unimodal with some mode $m$, then $m \le 16$ would force $z(G, 16) \ge z(G, 17)$, while $m \ge 16$ would force $z(G, 15) \le z(G, 16)$, both of which contradict the bounds. So a graph of order 20 has a non-unimodal zero forcing polynomial.
proof:
Three facts give the result. If $p\text{.coeff } b < p\text{.coeff } a$ and $p\text{.coeff } b < p\text{.coeff } c$ for $a < b < c$, then $p$ is not unimodal: a mode $m \ge b$ would give $p\text{.coeff } a \le p\text{.coeff } b$, and a mode $m \le b$ would give $p\text{.coeff } c \le p\text{.coeff } b$. It remains to prove $z(G,15) \ge 932$, $z(G,16) \le 909$ and $z(G,17) \ge 939$.

**From sets to their complements.** A set $S$ of size $k$ is counted by $z(G,k)$ exactly when its complement $W$, a set of $20-k$ white vertices, is cleared by the color change rule when all of $S$ starts blue. So $z(G,k)$ is the number of $(20-k)$-subsets $W$ of $\{0,\dots,19\}$ whose forcing process starting from the complement colors everything. The proof encodes $W$ as a 20-bit mask, and the graph as one natural number holding the 20 adjacency rows.

**A checked forcing procedure.** A computable procedure repeatedly looks for a blue vertex $v$ whose white neighbors, the mask $N(v) \wedge W$, form a single bit, and clears that bit. Two facts are proved about it in general, not by computation:

- *Soundness.* Every vertex that the procedure turns blue satisfies the inductive closure predicate. In particular, if the white mask becomes empty, then $S$ is a zero forcing set.
- *Completeness.* If the procedure stops with a nonempty white set $F$, then no blue vertex has exactly one neighbor in $F$, so $F$ is a fort. Induction on the closure predicate then shows that no vertex of $F$ is ever forced, so $S$ is not a zero forcing set.

To certify a stop quickly, the procedure computes the union $u_1$ of the neighborhoods of the white vertices and the set $u_2$ of vertices with at least two white neighbors. An invariant about these unions shows that if no blue vertex lies in $u_1$ but outside $u_2$, then no blue vertex has a single white neighbor.

**Counting.** Soundness gives a pointwise lower bound on the indicator of "zero forcing", and completeness gives a pointwise upper bound. A recursive enumerator sums these bounds over the $k$-subsets of $\{0,\dots,19\}$. It is proved equal to the corresponding sum over the binomial subsets of $\{0,\dots,19\}$, and it splits into partial sums by the largest elements of the subsets. Each partial sum is evaluated by the Lean kernel; the largest one covers 969 subsets.

- For $k = 17$, all 1140 sets of 3 white vertices are evaluated, giving $z(G,17) \ge 939$.
- For $k = 16$, the upper-bound sum over all 4845 sets of 4 white vertices is 909, giving $z(G,16) \le 909$.
- For $k = 15$, only a lower bound is needed. After a relabelling of the vertices, the 5-sets with good complements all have their two largest elements in 9 blocks covering 5221 of the 15504 five-sets. Those blocks alone give $z(G,15) \ge 932$.

With these three bounds the dip at 16 follows, and the existential statement is witnessed by $n = 20$ and this graph.
discussion:
The result formalized in theorem `op_1400_counterexample_order_le_eighty` resolves the specific question posed in Section 3, Question 2 of arXiv:2611.11352: whether there exists a graph of order at most 80 with a non-unimodal zero forcing polynomial. Before this, the smallest known example was the order-81 graph of arXiv:2611.11352; non-unimodal zero forcing polynomials already occur at order 20. The graph was found by a local search over blow-ups of small graphs, in which every vertex is replaced by a clique or an independent set of twins. Two white vertices in one twin class form a fort, so a good white set takes at most one vertex from each class, and the top coefficients become polynomials in the class sizes. The same search also found a graph of order 19 whose coefficients dip at index 15 ($780 > 754 < 780$). That example was checked by enumeration but is not formalized.

However, the result does not settle the broader question raised in Section 3, Question 2 of arXiv:2611.11352, which asks for the minimum order of a simple graph with a non-unimodal zero forcing polynomial. The Lean theorem gives the upper bound 20 on this minimum order (19 by the unformalized example). Whether smaller counterexamples exist is open. Specifically:

- Is the zero forcing polynomial $\mathcal{Z}(G; x)$ unimodal for all simple graphs $G$ of order $n \le 19$?
- What is the exact minimum order $n$ such that some simple graph of order $n$ has a non-unimodal zero forcing polynomial?

The theorem verifies a single instance; no enumeration of small graphs was done, so the exact minimum order is undetermined.

In addition to the order, the structural properties of graphs with non-unimodal zero forcing polynomials remain to be explored. In the order-20 graph the zero forcing number is 14, and the failure of unimodality occurs near the top of the spectrum, with coefficients dipping from degree 15 to degree 16 before rising again at degree 17. No general construction is given here, and no attempt is made to identify graph-theoretic characteristics—such as connectivity, maximum degree, or forbidden subgraphs—that necessitate or prevent non-unimodality. Determining the minimum order and identifying structural conditions under which zero forcing polynomials are guaranteed to be unimodal are the key open questions following from this work.
preliminaries:
We consider finite simple graphs and the formalization of their zero forcing polynomials in Lean 4. Throughout, a simple graph $G$ on a vertex type $V$ is represented by the Mathlib type SimpleGraph $V$, which consists of an irreflexive and symmetric binary relation $G\text{.Adj} : V \to V \to \text{Prop}$. For finite graphs, the vertex set is equipped with an instance of Fintype $V$. The zero forcing process, the zero forcing sets, the zero forcing polynomial, and unimodality are defined as follows.

Definition 1 (`ZeroForced`): Let $G$ be a simple graph on a type $V$, and let $S \subseteq V$ be a subset of vertices. The zero forcing closure of $S$ in $G$ is the subset of vertices colored by the iterative application of the color change rule. In Lean, this closure is formalized by the inductive predicate `ZeroForced` $G\ S : V \to \text{Prop}$, defined by two constructors:

- The constructor init states that every vertex in the initial seed set $S$ belongs to the closure: $v \in S \to \text{ZeroForced } G\, S\, v$.
- The constructor step states that if a vertex $u$ is already in the closure, $u$ is adjacent to $w$, and every neighbor $x$ of $u$ other than $w$ is already in the closure, then $w$ enters the closure: $\text{ZeroForced } G\, S\, u \to G\text{.Adj } u\, w \to (\forall x, G\text{.Adj } u\, x \to x \ne w \to \text{ZeroForced } G\, S\, x) \to \text{ZeroForced } G\, S\, w$.

Remark: The rule requires that all neighbors of $u$ except $w$ are already forced; once that condition holds, $w$ is forced in a single step.

Definition 2 (`is_zero_forcing_set`): Let $G$ be a simple graph on a type $V$, and let $S \subseteq V$ be a subset of vertices. The set $S$ is a zero forcing set of $G$ if its zero forcing closure contains all vertices of $G$. In Lean, this property is defined by `is_zero_forcing_set`:
$$\text{is\_zero\_forcing\_set}(G, S) \iff \forall v : V,\; \text{ZeroForced } G\, S\, v.$$
Here $S$ is viewed as a subset of type Set $V$, and the condition asserts that every vertex $v : V$ satisfies `ZeroForced` $G\ S\ v$.

Definition 3 (`zero_forcing_poly`): Let $V$ be a finite type equipped with Fintype $V$, and let $G$ be a simple graph on $V$. The zero forcing polynomial of $G$ is the generating function whose $k$-th coefficient is the number of zero forcing sets of cardinality $k$. In Lean, this is formalized as an element of Polynomial $\mathbb{N}$ via `zero_forcing_poly`:
$$\mathcal{Z}(G; X) = \sum_{S : \text{Finset } V} \text{if } \text{is\_zero\_forcing\_set}(G, S) \text{ then } X^{|S|} \text{ else } 0.$$
In Lean's definition of `zero_forcing_poly`, this corresponds to summing over all elements of Finset $V$.
Remark: The polynomial is defined over the natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ using Polynomial $\mathbb{N}$. Because decidability of `is_zero_forcing_set` is not assumed globally, the definition opens classical logic to define the indicator function via a conditional expression. The polynomial variable is the formal indeterminate Polynomial.X. Subsets are drawn from Finset $V$.

Definition 4 (`polynomial_is_unimodal`): A polynomial $p \in \text{Polynomial } \mathbb{N}$ with natural coefficients is unimodal if there exists a mode $m \in \mathbb{N}$ such that its coefficients weakly increase up to $m$ and weakly decrease thereafter. In Lean, this is defined by `polynomial_is_unimodal`:
$$\exists m : \mathbb{N},\; (\forall i \le j \le m,\; p\text{.coeff } i \le p\text{.coeff } j) \land (\forall m \le i \le j,\; p\text{.coeff } j \le p\text{.coeff } i).$$
Remark: Weak inequalities ($\le$) are used for both the non-decreasing and non-increasing phases. The mode $m$ is indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. In Mathlib, the coefficient $p\text{.coeff } k$ evaluates to 0 for any index $k$ exceeding the degree of $p$. Consequently, the weak monotonicity condition for $j \ge i \ge m$ holds naturally for indices past the degree, where all terms vanish.

problem.title: Order of the Smallest Graph with Non-Unimodal Zero Forcing Polynomial

research: Settles the order-at-most-80 question of OP-1400: an explicit graph on 20 vertices has a non-unimodal zero forcing polynomial (z(15) >= 932 > z(16) <= 909 < z(17) >= 939; exactly 420x^14+932x^15+909x^16+939x^17+180x^18+20x^19+x^20), far below the order-81 example of the source paper
tier_why: A single explicit counterexample (order 20) found by search: it answers the order-at-most-80 question and improves the known bound from 81 to 20, but determines neither the minimum order nor an infinite family.

zh.title: 具有非单峰零强迫多项式的20阶简单图的存在性
zh.abstract: 阶数为 $n$ 的图 $G$ 的零强迫（ZF）多项式 $\mathcal{Z}(G; x) = \sum_{i=1}^n z(G, i) x^i$ 按大小对其零强迫集进行计数。早先的工作提出了它是否总是单峰的这一问题；arXiv:2611.11352 通过一个无限族给出了否定的回答，该族中最小的成员阶数为 81，并询问了具有非单峰零强迫多项式的最小图是什么。我们给出了一个阶数为 20 的显式图，其零强迫多项式不是单峰的：Lean 证明了 $z(G,15) \ge 932$、$z(G,16) \le 909$ 以及 $z(G,17) \ge 939$，因此系数在 16 处出现下凹。穷举枚举给出了完整的多项式：$420x^{14}+932x^{15}+909x^{16}+939x^{17}+180x^{18}+20x^{19}+x^{20}$。这将最小阶数的已知上界从 81 降到了 20。
zh.introduction:
零强迫（ZF）是图上的一种动态过程，用于模拟信息或颜色在顶点间的传播。从染色的初始顶点子集开始，变色规则规定：恰好只有一个未染色邻点的已染色顶点会强迫该邻点变色。在此规则下的迭代闭包能染遍图中所有顶点的顶点子集被称为零强迫集。图的零强迫数是零强迫集的最小基数，它给出了与该图关联的对称矩阵的最大零度的界。

除了最小基数之外，所有零强迫集按大小的分布还提供了该图的详细组合特征。对于阶数 $n = |V|$ 的有限简单图 $G = (V, E)$，这种分布编码在零强迫多项式中：
$$\mathcal{Z}(G; x) = \sum_{i=1}^n z(G, i) x^i,$$
其中 $z(G, i)$ 表示 $G$ 的基数为 $i$ 的零强迫集的数量。多项式 $\mathcal{Z}(G; x)$ 是零强迫集的生成函数，对于所有严格小于 $G$ 的零强迫数的 $i$，均有 $z(G, i) = 0$，且由于全顶点集 $V$ 总是构成一个零强迫集，因此有 $z(G, n) = 1$。

组合多项式研究中的一个核心问题是单峰性。如果一个具有非负实系数的多项式的系数序列在达到最大指标（峰值（mode））之前非减，在此之后非增，则称该多项式是单峰的。许多经典的图多项式，例如匹配多项式、某些图类的独立多项式，以及在适当变换下的色多项式，都表现出单峰性或对数凹性。早先的工作询问了零强迫多项式 $\mathcal{Z}(G; x)$ 是否对每个有限简单图 $G$ 都是单峰的，该工作还证明了系数序列的前半部分始终是非减的。

在 arXiv:2611.11352 中证明了零强迫多项式一般不是单峰的。该论文引入了一个显式的构造族，并证明了记为 $G_{24,24,23}$ 的特定图阶数为 81 且具有非单峰的零强迫多项式。该族本身从 82 阶起都是非单峰的；而 81 阶图是它的一个较小变体。

arXiv:2611.11352 的第 3 节随后提出了问题 2：“具有非单峰零强迫多项式的最小图是什么？”这个 81 阶图是已知最小的例子，因此第一步是探究阶数至多为 80 的反例究竟是否存在。

本篇博文介绍了一个形式化验证，解决了阶数至多为 80 的问题。我们描述了在 Lean 4 证明助手中验证的定理 `op_1400_counterexample_order_le_eighty`，该定理证明了存在一个在 Fin $n$ 上的简单图 $G$，其中 $n \le 80$，其零强迫多项式不是单峰的。事实上，见证图的阶数为 $n = 20$，这远小于阈值 80 和原先 81 阶的反例。这个 20 顶点图的多项式为：
$$\mathcal{Z}(G; x) = 420 x^{14} + 932 x^{15} + 909 x^{16} + 939 x^{17} + 180 x^{18} + 20 x^{19} + x^{20}.$$
系数序列呈现出从 $z(G, 15) \ge 932$ 下降到 $z(G, 16) \le 909$，随后上升到 $z(G, 17) \ge 939$。这种内部下凹在数学上排除了单峰性。
zh.preliminaries:
我们考虑有限简单图及其在 Lean 4 中零强迫多项式的形式化。在全文中，顶点类型 $V$ 上的简单图 $G$ 由 Mathlib 类型 SimpleGraph $V$ 表示，它由反自反且对称的二元关系 $G\text{.Adj} : V \to V \to \text{Prop}$ 组成。对于有限图，顶点集配备了 Fintype $V$ 的实例。零强迫过程、零强迫集、零强迫多项式以及单峰性定义如下。

定义 1（`ZeroForced`）：设 $G$ 为类型 $V$ 上的简单图，并设 $S \subseteq V$ 为顶点子集。$S$ 在 $G$ 中的零强迫闭包是通过迭代应用变色规则染色的顶点子集。在 Lean 中，该闭包由归纳谓词 `ZeroForced` $G\ S : V \to \text{Prop}$ 形式化，由两个构造子定义：

- 构造子 init 指出初始种子集 $S$ 中的每个顶点都属于闭包：$v \in S \to \text{ZeroForced } G\, S\, v$。
- 构造子 step 指出若顶点 $u$ 已经在闭包中，$u$ 与 $w$ 相邻，且 $u$ 的除 $w$ 之外的每个邻点 $x$ 都已在闭包中，则 $w$ 进入闭包：$\text{ZeroForced } G\, S\, u \to G\text{.Adj } u\, w \to (\forall x, G\text{.Adj } u\, x \to x \ne w \to \text{ZeroForced } G\, S\, x) \to \text{ZeroForced } G\, S\, w$。

注：该规则要求除 $w$ 之外 $u$ 的所有邻点都已被强迫；一旦满足该条件，$w$ 便在单步内被强迫。

定义 2（`is_zero_forcing_set`）：设 $G$ 为类型 $V$ 上的简单图，并设 $S \subseteq V$ 为顶点子集。若 $S$ 的零强迫闭包包含 $G$ 的所有顶点，则集合 $S$ 是 $G$ 的一个零强迫集。在 Lean 中，此性质由 `is_zero_forcing_set` 定义：
$$\text{is\_zero\_forcing\_set}(G, S) \iff \forall v : V,\; \text{ZeroForced } G\, S\, v.$$
这里 $S$ 被视作 Set $V$ 类型的子集，该条件断言每个顶点 $v : V$ 都满足 `ZeroForced` $G\ S\ v$。

定义 3（`zero_forcing_poly`）：设 $V$ 为配备了 Fintype $V$ 的有限类型，设 $G$ 为 $V$ 上的简单图。$G$ 的零强迫多项式是以基数为 $k$ 的零强迫集数量作为其第 $k$ 个系数的生成函数。在 Lean 中，这通过 `zero_forcing_poly` 形式化为 Polynomial $\mathbb{N}$ 的一个元素：
$$\mathcal{Z}(G; X) = \sum_{S : \text{Finset } V} \text{if } \text{is\_zero\_forcing\_set}(G, S) \text{ then } X^{|S|} \text{ else } 0.$$
在 Lean 对 `zero_forcing_poly` 的定义中，这对应于对 Finset $V$ 的所有元素求和。
注：该多项式使用 Polynomial $\mathbb{N}$ 定义在自然数 $\mathbb{N}$ 上。因为没有在全局假定 `is_zero_forcing_set` 的可判定性，所以该定义开启了经典逻辑以通过条件表达式定义指示函数。多项式变量是形式不定元 Polynomial.X。子集取自 Finset $V$。

定义 4（`polynomial_is_unimodal`）：若具有自然数系数的多项式 $p \in \text{Polynomial } \mathbb{N}$ 存在一个峰值 $m \in \mathbb{N}$，使得其系数在达到 $m$ 之前弱递增且在此之后弱递减，则该多项式是单峰的。在 Lean 中，这由 `polynomial_is_unimodal` 定义：
$$\exists m : \mathbb{N},\; (\forall i \le j \le m,\; p\text{.coeff } i \le p\text{.coeff } j) \land (\forall m \le i \le j,\; p\text{.coeff } j \le p\text{.coeff } i).$$
注：在非减阶段和非增阶段均使用弱不等式（$\le$）。峰值 $m$ 以 $\mathbb{N}$ 为指标。在 Mathlib 中，对于超过 $p$ 的次数的任意指标 $k$，系数 $p\text{.coeff } k$ 均求值为 0。因此，对于超过次数的指标，所有项都变为 0，从而 $j \ge i \ge m$ 的弱单调性条件自然成立。
zh.result:
主定理通过给出一个阶数为 20 的显式反例解决了阶数至多为 80 的问题。

定理（`op_1400_counterexample_order_le_eighty`）：
存在自然数 $n \le 80$ 以及顶点集 Fin $n$ 上邻接关系可判定的简单图 $G$，其零强迫多项式不是单峰的：
$$\exists (n : \mathbb{N})\; (\_ : n \le 80)\; (G : \text{SimpleGraph } (\text{Fin } n))\; (\_ : \text{DecidableRel } G.\text{Adj}),\; \neg\, \text{polynomial_is_unimodal } (\text{zero_forcing_poly } G).$$

Lean 陈述 `op_1400_counterexample_order_le_eighty` 通过对自然数 $n$、不等式约束 $n \le 80$、类型 Fin $n$ 上的简单图 $G$ 以及可判定邻接实例 DecidableRel $G\text{.Adj}$ 进行存在量化来解读该英文定理，断言按照 `polynomial_is_unimodal`，零强迫多项式 `zero_forcing_poly` $G$ 不是单峰的。

见证图 $G$ 具有顶点集 $\{0, \dots, 19\}$ 和 135 条边：两个不同的顶点均相邻，除非它们构成以下 55 对之一，
$${0,1}, {0,4}, {0,5}, {0,6}, {0,8}, {0,9}, {1,8}, {1,9}, {2,3}, {2,7}, {2,8}, {2,9}, {3,7}, {3,8}, {3,9}, {4,5}, {4,6}, {4,7}, {5,6}, {5,7}, {6,7}, {10,11}, {10,12}, {10,13}, {10,14}, {10,15}, {10,16}, {10,17}, {11,12}, {11,13}, {11,14}, {11,15}, {11,16}, {11,17}, {12,13}, {12,14}, {12,15}, {12,16}, {12,17}, {13,15}, {13,16}, {13,17}, {13,19}, {14,15}, {14,16}, {14,17}, {14,19}, {15,16}, {15,17}, {15,18}, {15,19}, {16,17}, {16,18}, {16,19}, {17,18}.$$
它的孪生类（在该对之外具有相同邻点的顶点）为 $\{2,3\}$、$\{4,5,6\}$、$\{8,9\}$、$\{10,11,12\}$、$\{13,14\}$、$\{15,16\}$ 以及六个单元素集，因此 $G$ 是一个 12 顶点图的吹胀。通过穷举枚举（Lean 之外的计算），其零强迫多项式为：
$$\mathcal{Z}(G; X) = 420 X^{14} + 932 X^{15} + 909 X^{16} + 939 X^{17} + 180 X^{18} + 20 X^{19} + X^{20}.$$
因此其零强迫数为 14。Lean 并没有证明这些精确值；它证明了以下三个界，而这些界正是确立非单峰性所需的全部内容。

$G$ 的非单峰性由次数为 15、16 和 17 处的三个系数所见证，它们满足：
$$z(G, 15) \ge 932,\quad z(G, 16) \le 909,\quad z(G, 17) \ge 939.$$
由于 $z(G, 15) > z(G, 16)$ 且 $z(G, 16) < z(G, 17)$，系数序列在指标 16 处严格下凹。若该多项式是以某个 $m$ 为峰值的单峰多项式，则 $m \le 16$ 会迫使 $z(G, 16) \ge z(G, 17)$，而 $m \ge 16$ 会迫使 $z(G, 15) \le z(G, 16)$，这两者都与上述界矛盾。因此，存在一个阶数为 20 的图，其零强迫多项式不是单峰的。
zh.proof:
三个事实给出了该结果。若对于 $a < b < c$ 有 $p\text{.coeff } b < p\text{.coeff } a$ 以及 $p\text{.coeff } b < p\text{.coeff } c$，则 $p$ 不是单峰的：峰值 $m \ge b$ 会导致 $p\text{.coeff } a \le p\text{.coeff } b$，而峰值 $m \le b$ 会导致 $p\text{.coeff } c \le p\text{.coeff } b$。接下来只需证明 $z(G,15) \ge 932$、$z(G,16) \le 909$ 以及 $z(G,17) \ge 939$。

**从集合到其补集。** 大小为 $k$ 的集合 $S$ 被 $z(G,k)$ 计入，恰好当以 $S$ 中的所有顶点最初为蓝色开始时，其补集 $W$（由 $20-k$ 个白色顶点组成的集合）被变色规则完全清除。因此，$z(G,k)$ 是 $\{0,\dots,19\}$ 的 $(20-k)$ 元子集 $W$ 的数量，使得从其补集开始的强迫过程染遍所有顶点。该证明将 $W$ 编码为一个 20 位掩码，并将图编码为保存 20 个邻接行的一个自然数。

**经检验的强迫程序。** 一个可计算程序反复寻找白色邻点（即掩码 $N(v) \wedge W$）仅构成单个位的蓝色顶点 $v$，并清除该位。关于该程序在一般情况下证明了两个事实，而不是通过计算证明的：

- *可靠性。* 程序变为蓝色的每个顶点都满足归纳闭包谓词。特别是，如果白色掩码变为空，则 $S$ 是一个零强迫集。
- *完备性。* 如果程序停止于非空白色集合 $F$，则没有蓝色顶点在 $F$ 中恰好只有一个邻点，因此 $F$ 是一个堡垒（fort）。对闭包谓词进行归纳表明 $F$ 中的任何顶点都不会被强迫，因此 $S$ 不是零强迫集。

为了快速认证停止，该程序计算白色顶点邻域的并集 $u_1$ 以及至少具有两个白色邻点的顶点集 $u_2$。关于这些并集的一个不变量表明，若没有蓝色顶点位于 $u_1$ 中但处于 $u_2$ 之外，则没有蓝色顶点具有恰好一个白色邻点。

**计数。** 可靠性给出了“零强迫”指示函数的逐点下界，而完备性给出了逐点上界。一个递归枚举器在 $\{0,\dots,19\}$ 的 $k$ 元子集上对这些界求和。它被证明等于 $\{0,\dots,19\}$ 的二项式子集上的相应和，并且它按子集的最大元素拆分为若干部分和。每个部分和均由 Lean 内核求值；最大的一个覆盖了 969 个子集。

- 对于 $k = 17$，求值了所有 1140 个由 3 个白色顶点组成的集合，得出 $z(G,17) \ge 939$。
- 对于 $k = 16$，在所有 4845 个由 4 个白色顶点组成的集合上的上界和为 909，得出 $z(G,16) \le 909$。
- 对于 $k = 15$，仅需要下界。在对顶点重新标号后，具有良好补集的 5 元集的最大两个元素均落在覆盖 15504 个 5 元集中 5221 个的 9 个块中。仅这些块就给出了 $z(G,15) \ge 932$。

有了这三个界，16 处的下凹便得以确立，存在性陈述由 $n = 20$ 和该图所见证。
zh.discussion:
在定理 `op_1400_counterexample_order_le_eighty` 中形式化的结果解决了 arXiv:2611.11352 第 3 节问题 2 中提出的具体问题：是否存在阶数至多为 80 且具有非单峰零强迫多项式的图。在此之前，已知最小的例子是 arXiv:2611.11352 中的 81 阶图；非单峰零强迫多项式在 20 阶时就已出现。该图是通过在小图的吹胀上进行局部搜索发现的，其中每个顶点都被替换为一个团或由孪生顶点组成的独立集。同一个孪生类中的两个白色顶点会构成一个堡垒，因此一个好的白色集合从每个类中至多选取一个顶点，而最高项系数变成了关于各类大小的多项式。相同的搜索还发现了一个 19 阶图，其系数在指标 15 处出现下凹（$780 > 754 < 780$）。该例子已通过枚举进行检验，但未被形式化。

然而，该结果并未解决 arXiv:2611.11352 第 3 节问题 2 提出的更广泛的问题，即寻找具有非单峰零强迫多项式的简单图的最小阶数。Lean 定理给出了该最小阶数的上界 20（根据未形式化的例子为 19）。是否存在更小的反例仍是未决的。具体而言：

- 对于阶数 $n \le 19$ 的所有简单图 $G$，零强迫多项式 $\mathcal{Z}(G; x)$ 是否都是单峰的？
- 使得某个 $n$ 阶简单图具有非单峰零强迫多项式的确切最小阶数 $n$ 是多少？

该定理验证了单个实例；由于未对小图进行枚举，因此确切的最小阶数仍未确定。

除阶数之外，具有非单峰零强迫多项式的图的结构性质仍有待探索。在 20 阶图中，零强迫数为 14，单峰性的破坏发生在谱的高端，系数从 15 次下降到 16 次，随后在 17 次再次上升。本文未给出通用的构造，也未试图确定导致或阻止非单峰性的图论特征——例如连通度、最大度或禁用子图。确定最小阶数以及找出保证零强迫多项式为单峰的结构条件，是本项工作引出的关键公开问题。
